title: White Rice vs Brown Rice: Nutrition Differences

seo.title: White vs Brown Rice: Fiber, Calories and Nutrients
seo.meta_description: White and brown rice have similar calories, carbs and protein. Brown rice retains bran and germ, so it provides more fiber and magnesium.
seo.search_intent: Compare cooked white and brown rice with like-for-like numbers and explain what refining actually changes.

excerpt: Cooked white and brown rice provide similar amounts of calories, carbohydrate and protein. The important difference is that brown rice keeps the bran and germ: it has roughly 1.5–2 grams of fiber per 100 grams versus less than 1 gram in white rice and usually provides more magnesium and other micronutrients.
content_html:
Brown rice is often presented as nutritionally opposite to white rice, but once both are cooked they are still, above all, carbohydrate-rich grain foods. Calories and protein do not change dramatically.

The most consistent difference is fiber and the parts of the grain that remain. Brown rice keeps the bran and germ; white rice loses those layers during milling.

A cooked comparison per 100 grams

The amount of water absorbed changes values somewhat across varieties and cooking methods, so these are representative rather than universal numbers.

Per 100 g cookedWhite riceBrown rice
Calories~130~120–125
Carbohydrate~28 g~25–26 g
Protein~2.7 g~2.7–2.8 g
Fiber~0.4 g~1.6 g

Calories and protein are very close. Fiber is the clearer difference: brown rice provides about four times as much in this comparison, though the absolute amount per 100 grams is still moderate.

A same-weight serving makes the fiber gap easier to see

In 5 ounces cooked, white rice provides roughly 185 calories, about 40 grams of carbohydrate and well under 1 gram of fiber. The same weight of brown rice provides roughly 175 calories, 36 grams of carbohydrate and about 2.3 grams of fiber.

The small calorie difference can shift with variety and hydration. The fiber advantage of brown rice is much more consistent.

What milling removes

A whole grain contains endosperm, germ and bran. Making white rice removes the bran and germ, reducing fiber along with some vitamins and minerals.

In the United States, many white rice products are enriched with B vitamins and iron after milling. Enrichment can replace selected nutrients, but it does not restore the fiber or recreate the whole grain.

Brown rice usually provides more magnesium

Cooked brown rice can provide roughly 40–45 mg of magnesium per 100 grams, while white rice is often closer to 10–15 mg. Across a 5-ounce serving, that can mean around 60 mg versus less than 20 mg.

That mineral difference matters more nutritionally than arguing over five or ten calories.

Neither rice is a major protein food

At roughly 2.7 grams per 100 grams, a 5-ounce serving supplies about 4 grams of protein either way. If a meal needs 20–30 grams, switching from white to brown rice will not solve that; beans, tofu, eggs, fish, meat, dairy or another protein source will do much more.

Brown rice may be more filling, but the meal still matters

Its extra fiber and firmer texture can slow eating and make a meal feel somewhat more filling. Satiety, however, also depends on portion size and what is eaten with the rice.

White rice served with vegetables and a substantial protein source can be more filling than brown rice eaten by itself.

Brown rice usually takes longer to cook

The bran layer slows water penetration, so brown rice generally needs more cooking time. That same retained layer is part of why it contains more fiber and has a firmer texture.

The useful rule

Brown rice is not low-carb, and white rice is not nutritionally empty. They are similar in energy and protein; brown rice has a clear advantage in fiber and several micronutrients. Which one fits better can also depend on the dish, texture preference and the rest of the diet.

faq.question: Which has more calories, white or brown rice?
faq.answer: Cooked, they are very close. White rice is around 130 calories/100 g and brown rice roughly 120–125, but variety and hydration can shift the numbers.

faq.question: Which has more fiber?
faq.answer: Brown rice clearly: about 1.6 g/100 g versus roughly 0.4 g/100 g in representative cooked white rice.

faq.question: Does brown rice have more protein?
faq.answer: Only trivially. Both are around 2.7–2.8 grams of protein per 100 grams cooked.
